title: Compound Probability
seo_title: Grade 7 Compound Probability Worksheets: Sample Spaces, Tree Diagrams and Independent Events
standard_text: Find probabilities of compound events using organized lists, tables, tree diagrams, and simulation.
meta_desc: Free Grade 7 compound probability worksheets: sample spaces with lists, tables and tree diagrams, the counting principle, independent events, with and without replacement, simulations and word problems. 100 practice questions with an answer key.
key_big: Count outcomes by multiplying. For independent events, multiply the probabilities.
key_sub: Coin and number cube: 2 × 6 = 12 outcomes. P(heads and 4) = 1/2 × 1/6 = 1/12.
body_html:
Sample spaces

A compound event is made of two or more events. Its sample space is every possible outcome. Show it with a list, a table or a tree diagram. To count outcomes, multiply the number of choices at each step.

Way to show itExampleOutcomes
ListCoin + coinHH, HT, TH, TT
TableTwo number cubes6 rows × 6 columns = 36
Tree diagramShirt (3) then pants (4)3 × 4 = 12 paths

Probability of a compound event

P = favorable outcomes ÷ all outcomes. For independent events (one does not change the other), multiply: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).

Example

Flip a coin and roll a number cube. What is P(heads and 4)?

2 × 6 = 12 outcomes. Only H4 works.

Or multiply: 12 × 16 = 112.

Answer: 112

Example

A bag has 3 red and 2 blue marbles. Pick one, keep it, pick again. P(red, red)?

35 × 24 = 620 = 310.

Answer: 310

Common mistakes

  • Adding instead of multiplying: 3 shirts and 4 pants make 12 outfits, not 7.
  • Counting HT and TH as one outcome.
  • Forgetting that without replacement, the second draw has one fewer item.

faq.a: An event made of two or more simple events, like flipping heads and rolling a 4.

faq.q: How do you find the number of outcomes?
faq.a: Multiply the number of choices at each step. 3 shirts and 4 pants make 3 × 4 = 12 outfits.

faq.q: How do you find the probability of two independent events?
faq.a: Multiply their probabilities: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).
After the first pick, there is one fewer item, so the second probability changes. With 3 red and 2 blue, P(red, red) = 3/5 × 2/4.

items.q: You flip a coin and roll a number cube. How many outcomes are in the sample space?
items.e: Multiply the choices: 2 × 6 = 12 outcomes. Not 8: adding counts only one choice at a time.

items.q: You choose a shirt (3 colors) and pants (4 colors). How many outcomes are in the sample space?
items.e: Multiply the choices: 3 × 4 = 12 outcomes. Not 7: adding counts only one choice at a time.

items.q: You spin a spinner with 5 equal parts and flip a coin. How many outcomes are in the sample space?
items.e: Multiply the choices: 5 × 2 = 10 outcomes. Not 7: adding counts only one choice at a time.

items.q: You pick a sandwich (4 kinds) and a drink (3 kinds). How many outcomes are in the sample space?
items.e: Multiply the choices: 4 × 3 = 12 outcomes. Not 7: adding counts only one choice at a time.

items.q: You roll two number cubes. How many outcomes are in the sample space?
items.e: Multiply the choices: 6 × 6 = 36 outcomes. Not 12: adding counts only one choice at a time.

items.q: You pick a letter from A, B, C and a number from 1 to 5. How many outcomes are in the sample space?
items.e: Multiply the choices: 3 × 5 = 15 outcomes. Not 8: adding counts only one choice at a time.

items.q: You choose a size (small, medium, large) and a flavor (6 flavors). How many outcomes are in the sample space?
items.e: Multiply the choices: 3 × 6 = 18 outcomes. Not 9: adding counts only one choice at a time.

items.q: You flip a coin three times. How many outcomes are in the sample space?
items.e: Each flip has 2 outcomes: 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 outcomes (HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT, THH, THT, TTH, TTT).

items.q: Which list is the sample space for flipping two coins?
items.e: HT (first heads, then tails) and TH are different outcomes. There are 4.

items.q: A tree diagram shows 3 branches, and each has 4 branches. How many outcomes are at the ends?
items.e: 3 × 4 = 12 branch ends.

items.q: What is a compound event?
c: Any event with a number cube
An event made of two or more simple events, like rolling a 6 and flipping heads
An event that can never happen
items.e: A compound event combines two or more events.

items.q: A menu has 3 soups, 5 main dishes and 2 desserts. How many meals of one soup, one main and one dessert are possible?
A lock code uses 3 digits, each 0 to 9. How many codes are possible?
An outfit has a hat (2 choices), a shirt (3 choices) and shoes (4 choices). How many outfits are possible?
items.e: 2 × 3 × 4 = 24 outfits.

items.q: An outfit has a hat (4 choices), a shirt (2 choices) and shoes (5 choices). How many outfits are possible?
items.e: 4 × 2 × 5 = 40 outfits.

items.q: An outfit has a hat (3 choices), a shirt (3 choices) and shoes (2 choices). How many outfits are possible?
items.e: 3 × 3 × 2 = 18 outfits.

items.q: An outfit has a hat (2 choices), a shirt (2 choices) and shoes (6 choices). How many outfits are possible?
items.e: 2 × 2 × 6 = 24 outfits.

items.q: An outfit has a hat (5 choices), a shirt (4 choices) and shoes (2 choices). How many outfits are possible?
items.e: 5 × 4 × 2 = 40 outfits.

items.q: An outfit has a hat (6 choices), a shirt (2 choices) and shoes (2 choices). How many outfits are possible?
items.e: 6 × 2 × 2 = 24 outfits.

items.q: An outfit has a hat (3 choices), a shirt (4 choices) and shoes (5 choices). How many outfits are possible?
items.e: 3 × 4 × 5 = 60 outfits.

items.q: You roll two number cubes (36 outcomes). What is P(a sum of 7)?
items.e: 6 of the 36 outcomes work: 6/36 = 1/6.

items.q: You roll two number cubes (36 outcomes). What is P(a sum of 12)?
items.e: 1 of the 36 outcomes work: 1/36.

items.q: You roll two number cubes (36 outcomes). What is P(doubles (the same number on both))?
items.e: 6 of the 36 outcomes work: 6/36 = 1/6.

items.q: You roll two number cubes (36 outcomes). What is P(a sum of 10)?
items.e: 3 of the 36 outcomes work: 3/36 = 1/12.

items.q: You roll two number cubes (36 outcomes). What is P(a sum less than 4)?
items.e: 3 of the 36 outcomes work: 3/36 = 1/12.

items.q: You roll two number cubes (36 outcomes). What is P(a sum of 2 or 3)?
items.e: 3 of the 36 outcomes work: 3/36 = 1/12.

items.q: You roll two number cubes (36 outcomes). What is P(an even sum)?
items.e: 18 of the 36 outcomes work: 18/36 = 1/2.

items.q: You roll two number cubes (36 outcomes). What is P(a sum of 8)?
items.e: 5 of the 36 outcomes work: 5/36.

items.q: You flip a coin 3 times (8 outcomes). What is P(exactly 2 heads)?
items.e: List the 8 outcomes: HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT, THH, THT, TTH, TTT. 3 of them work: 3/8.

items.q: You flip a coin 3 times (8 outcomes). What is P(at least 1 head)?
items.e: List the 8 outcomes: HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT, THH, THT, TTH, TTT. 7 of them work: 7/8.

items.q: You flip a coin 3 times (8 outcomes). What is P(no heads)?
items.e: List the 8 outcomes: HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT, THH, THT, TTH, TTT. 1 of them work: 1/8.

items.q: You flip a coin 3 times (8 outcomes). What is P(all three the same)?
items.e: List the 8 outcomes: HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT, THH, THT, TTH, TTT. 2 of them work: 2/8.

items.q: You flip a coin and roll a number cube (12 outcomes). What is P(heads and a 4)?
items.e: Count the outcomes that work out of 12, or multiply: P = 112.

items.q: You flip a coin and roll a number cube (12 outcomes). What is P(tails and an even number)?
items.e: Count the outcomes that work out of 12, or multiply: P = 14.

items.q: You flip a coin and roll a number cube (12 outcomes). What is P(heads and a number greater than 4)?
items.e: Count the outcomes that work out of 12, or multiply: P = 16.

items.q: You flip a coin and roll a number cube (12 outcomes). What is P(tails and a 1 or a 2)?
items.e: Count the outcomes that work out of 12, or multiply: P = 16.

items.q: A spinner has red, blue and green (equal parts). You spin twice. What is P(red both times)?
items.e: 3 × 3 = 9 outcomes, and only red-red works: 1/9.

items.q: A spinner has red, blue and green (equal parts). You spin twice. What is P(the same color both times)?
items.e: RR, BB and GG: 3 of 9 outcomes = 1/3.

items.q: You pick one of A, B, C and flip a coin. What is P(A and heads)?
items.e: 3 × 2 = 6 outcomes. Only A-heads works: 1/6.

items.q: A bag has 1 red and 1 blue cube. You pick one, put it back, then pick again. What is P(two different colors)?
items.e: Outcomes: RR, RB, BR, BB. RB and BR work: 2/4 = 1/2.

items.q: P(a coin lands heads) = 12 and P(a number cube shows 3) = 16. The events are independent. What is the probability that both happen?
items.e: Multiply: 12 × 16 = 112. Not 23: adding gives the wrong answer for both events.

items.q: P(a spinner lands on blue) = 14 and P(you draw a red card from 1 red and 2 black) = 13. The events are independent. What is the probability that both happen?
items.e: Multiply: 14 × 13 = 112. Not 712: adding gives the wrong answer for both events.

items.q: P(you pick a green marble (2 of 5)) = 25 and P(a coin lands tails) = 12. The events are independent. What is the probability that both happen?
items.e: Multiply: 25 × 12 = 15. Not 910: adding gives the wrong answer for both events.

items.q: P(it is sunny on Monday) = 34 and P(it is sunny on Tuesday (independent)) = 23. The events are independent. What is the probability that both happen?
items.e: Multiply: 34 × 23 = 12. Not a number over 1: adding gives the wrong answer for both events.

items.q: P(the first cube shows 6) = 16 and P(the second cube shows 6) = 16. The events are independent. What is the probability that both happen?
items.e: Multiply: 16 × 16 = 136. Not 13: adding gives the wrong answer for both events.

items.q: P(the first coin is heads) = 12 and P(the second coin is heads) = 12. The events are independent. What is the probability that both happen?
items.e: Multiply: 12 × 12 = 14. Not 1: adding gives the wrong answer for both events.

items.q: P(you win a game (3 in 10)) = 310 and P(a coin lands heads) = 12. The events are independent. What is the probability that both happen?
items.e: Multiply: 310 × 12 = 320. Not 45: adding gives the wrong answer for both events.

items.q: P(the first cube is not a 6) = 56 and P(the second cube is not a 6) = 56. The events are independent. What is the probability that both happen?
items.e: Multiply: 56 × 56 = 2536. Not a number over 1: adding gives the wrong answer for both events.

items.q: P(a spinner lands on 1 (of 5)) = 15 and P(a different spinner lands on A, B or C (of 4)) = 34. The events are independent. What is the probability that both happen?
items.e: Multiply: 15 × 34 = 320. Not 1920: adding gives the wrong answer for both events.

items.q: P(you pick a vowel from A, E, T) = 23 and P(you draw a heart (1/4)) = 14. The events are independent. What is the probability that both happen?
items.e: Multiply: 23 × 14 = 16. Not 1112: adding gives the wrong answer for both events.

items.q: Each try has probability 12 and the tries are independent. What is the probability of success 3 times in a row?
items.e: Multiply 3 times: (12)3 = 18.

items.q: Each try has probability 12 and the tries are independent. What is the probability of success 4 times in a row?
items.e: Multiply 4 times: (12)4 = 116.

items.q: Each try has probability 16 and the tries are independent. What is the probability of success 2 times in a row?
items.e: Multiply 2 times: (16)2 = 136.

items.q: Each try has probability 13 and the tries are independent. What is the probability of success 2 times in a row?
items.e: Multiply 2 times: (13)2 = 19.

items.q: Each try has probability 12 and the tries are independent. What is the probability of success 5 times in a row?
items.e: Multiply 5 times: (12)5 = 132.

items.q: Which events are independent?
c: Drawing two cards without putting the first back
Picking two marbles without replacing the first
Picking two students for two jobs from the same group, without repeats
Flipping a coin and rolling a number cube
items.e: One result does not change the other. Without replacement, the second draw depends on the first.

items.q: A bag has 3 red and 2 blue marbles. You pick one, put it back, then pick again. What is P(red, then red)?
items.e: With replacement: 3/5 × 3/5 = 9/25.

items.q: A bag has 3 red and 2 blue marbles. You pick one and keep it, then pick again. What is P(red, then red)?
items.e: Without replacement: 3/5 × 2/4 = 6/20 = 3/10.

items.q: A spinner is half red and half blue. You spin it twice. Which is more likely?
c: One red and one blue (in any order)
items.e: RB and BR give 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2. RR and BB are 1/4 each.

A tree diagram shows a coin flip (H or T), then a spinner (1, 2 or 3). How many outcomes are there?
A tree diagram shows 2 drinks, then 3 snacks, then 2 desserts. How many paths are there?
A tree shows heads/tails, then a number cube. How many paths end in heads and an odd number?
items.e: Heads, then 1, 3 or 5: 3 paths.

items.q: A tree has 4 first branches and 4 second branches on each. How many paths have the same choice twice?
items.e: AA, BB, CC, DD: 4 paths out of 16.

items.q: A coin is flipped twice. What is P(at least one head)?
items.e: HH, HT, TH work: 3/4. Or 1 − P(TT) = 1 − 1/4.

items.q: Two number cubes are rolled. What is P(at least one 6)?
items.e: 6 outcomes have a 6 first, 6 have a 6 second, and 6-6 is counted twice: 6 + 6 − 1 = 11. 11/36.

items.q: A family has 3 children. Assuming boys and girls are equally likely, what is P(at least one girl)?
items.e: Only BBB has no girl: 1 − 1/8 = 7/8.

items.q: You guess on 2 true/false questions. What is P(both right)?
You guess on 3 multiple-choice questions with 4 choices each. What is P(all 3 right)?
To simulate a 50% chance, which tool works?
c: Roll a number cube and use 1 only
Spin a spinner with 3 equal parts
items.e: A fair coin gives heads half the time, matching 50%.

items.q: A player makes 1 out of 6 shots. Which simulation fits?
c: Pick from 10 cards; 1 to 6 means a make
Flip a coin; heads means a make
Roll a number cube; a 1 means a make
items.e: A number cube gives 1 with probability 1/6.

items.q: In a simulation of 50 trials, the event happened 12 times. What is the estimated probability?
items.e: Estimate = times it happened ÷ trials = 12/50 = 0.24.

items.q: Which gives a better estimate from a simulation?
items.e: More trials usually give an estimate closer to the true probability.

items.q: A cereal box has 1 of 4 prizes. To simulate buying boxes, a student spins a spinner with 4 equal parts. What does one spin stand for?
c: The number of boxes you need
items.e: Each spin picks one of 4 equally likely prizes, like opening one box.

items.q: A simulation for 'a family with 2 children' uses two coin flips. What does HT stand for?
c: A boy first, then a girl (if H = boy)
items.e: Each flip stands for one child, in order.

items.q: A café has 4 sandwiches and 3 drinks. One combo is picked at random. What is P(the turkey sandwich and lemonade)?
items.e: 4 × 3 = 12 combos, and 1 works: 1/12.

Ana rolls two number cubes. What is P(the sum is 9)?

You flip a coin 4 times. What is P(all heads)?
A game spinner lands on 'win' 1/3 of the time. What is P(you lose two spins in a row)?
A test has 2 multiple-choice questions with 5 choices each. A student guesses. What is P(both wrong)?
A restaurant has 5 main dishes and 4 desserts. You pick one of each at random. What is P(pasta and cake)?
A drawer has 4 black and 4 white socks. You take one, keep it, then take another. What is P(both black)?
Two friends each pick a number from 1 to 5. What is P(they pick the same number)?
items.e: 25 pairs, and 5 match: 5/25 = 1/5.

items.q: A weather app says 40% chance of rain each day for 2 days (independent). What is P(no rain on both days)?
A coin is flipped and a 4-section spinner (red, blue, green, yellow) is spun. How many outcomes have heads or red?
items.e: Heads with any color: 4. Tails with red: 1. Total 5.

items.q: A class picks a president and a vice president from 5 students (different people). How many ways?
items.e: 5 choices, then 4: 5 × 4 = 20.

items.q: A machine part fails 1 in 50 times. Two parts are used and work independently. What is P(neither fails)?
A spinner has 3 equal parts: A, B, C. You spin 3 times. What is P(A, B, C in that order)?
